title: Headaches, Low Libido and a Lorry Licence / Test Fields, Check Hormones, Tell DVLA

blocks.text: Headaches, Low Libido and a Lorry Licence / Test Fields, Check Hormones, Tell DVLA

AMaC MRCP PACES · R3-31 · Consultation · PACES Consultation (Station 5) · Skills A, B, C, D, E, F, G · 20 minutes (15 with the patient, then 5 of examiner questions; warning at 13 minutes) · Guidelines: Endocrine Society: Diagnosis and treatment of hyperprolactinemia (2011); Endocrine Society: Hormonal replacement in hypopituitarism in adults (2016); DVLA: Visual disorders, assessing fitness to drive (last updated 26 September 2025); GMC: Confidentiality: patients' fitness to drive and reporting concerns to the DVLA or DVA (2017) · Related AMaC: None identified
Dear Doctor, a 41-year-old lorry driver. Six months of headaches, tiredness and loss of sex drive, and he thinks he has been bumping into things. Blood pressure 128/80. Please assess and advise.
The patient has consented to see you. Please take a history, perform a relevant examination and explain your assessment and plan to the patient.

sections.heading: 4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap

blocks.text: The Hook. Headache, low libido and a visual field loss together point to a pituitary tumour pressing on the optic chiasm. The most likely cause of the raised prolactin is a prolactinoma, which usually responds to a tablet rather than an operation.

The Examiner Trap. He drives a lorry for a living and fears an operation. Candidates treat the hormones and forget his licence, or send him straight to surgery. Pass: fields, hormones, cabergoline, DVLA. Fail: no driving advice.

rows: Ask about the headache and vision, then about the sex drive, and then ask what he drives.
"Where is the headache? Have you noticed losing sight at the sides? What do you drive?"
Headache; vision; erections; libido; fatigue; breast changes; medicines; weight; drive; partner.
Test the visual fields and look for lost hormones.
"May I test your sight at the edges, look at your eyes and check your blood pressure lying and standing? Tell me if anything hurts."
Fields to confrontation; acuity; fundi; eye movements; hair; testes; lying and standing pressure; cover him.
Name the diagnosis, say what blood tests and scans you need, explain the tablet, and give clear driving advice.
"I think a growth on the pituitary gland is pressing on the nerves for your sight. You must stop driving until the DVLA advise."
Prolactin; other hormones; MRI; fields; cabergoline; DVLA; red flags; follow-up.
No introduction or consent; examines without asking; leaves him exposed.
Introduces self, asks consent, asks about discomfort before examining, covers him and thanks him.
Also offers a chaperone and asks permission before sensitive questions about sexual function.
Asks about headache only; omits vision, libido, medicines or his job.
Asks headache, vision, erections, libido, tiredness, breast changes, medicines, and what he drives.
Also asks about a partner, fertility, thirst, and whether he has had a recent fall or crash.
Omits visual fields or fundi; reports defects that are absent.
Finds a bitemporal field loss to confrontation, normal fundi, reduced facial hair, small soft testes and normal eye movements.
Also finds no galactorrhoea, normal acuity and no postural fall, and reports acromegalic features as absent.
Pituitary macroadenoma pressing on the chiasm, most likely a prolactinoma, with hypopituitarism.
Also names a non-functioning adenoma with a raised prolactin from stalk compression, and medicines as a cause.
Asks for prolactin, testosterone with LH and FSH, 9 am cortisol, TSH and free T4, IGF-1, and a pituitary MRI.
Also asks for formal visual fields, baseline echocardiography before cabergoline, and a short Synacthen test because the 9 am cortisol is indeterminate.
Critical fail (AMaC practice flag, not an official automatic PACES fail): says he can keep driving, or does not tell him to seek emergency help for sudden severe headache with visual loss.

Says stop driving (lorry and car) and tell DVLA, start cabergoline if confirmed, assess the adrenal axis before starting thyroxine (hydrocortisone cover first if that cannot be done promptly), and call 999 for sudden severe headache.
Also says the duty to tell DVLA is his and the doctor may disclose if he refuses (GMC), and that surgery is for failure of tablets or a threatened sight.
Brushes aside his fear of surgery and of losing his job.
Asks what worries him, acknowledges both fears and answers honestly, including that a tablet is usually tried first.
Also offers a letter for his employer and occupational health, and asks about money and his family.
Tells him what to do with no choices.
Explains tests with a tablet trial, or tests with early surgical review, and asks his choice.
Records his choice, gives a written summary and a dated follow-up with fields repeated.

blocks.text: High-performance is an AMaC teaching label, not an official grade. It shows what lifts a pass from adequate to convincing. Critical fail is an AMaC practice flag for an action that could harm the patient today; it is not an official automatic PACES fail.
Who you are: A 41-year-old lorry driver for a haulage firm. You are practical, a little embarrassed about sexual problems, and anxious about money.
Opening line: "Doc, my head's been banging for months, I'm knackered, and the wife says I'm not interested any more. I keep catching the wing mirror on things."
Volunteered: six months. A dull headache across the forehead. Tired all day. Libido gone.

Only if asked: your erections are poor and you shave less. No breast changes. No thirst or passing a lot of urine. You do not smoke; a couple of pints at weekends; no allergies; no family history of pituitary or hormone problems; married with two children. You have not noticed a clear loss of sight but you miss things on both sides. You take no regular tablets.
Only if asked what you drive: a heavy lorry, long distance, about five days a week. You have not told your firm. You nearly clipped a van last week.
Hidden concern (only if asked what worries you): you are terrified of an operation on your brain and of losing your licence and your job. Say: "If I can't drive, we lose the house."
Your questions, in your own words: "Is it a brain tumour?" "Will I need an operation?" "Can I carry on driving?"
How you react: if told to stop driving with no support, you say you will carry on. If listened to and offered a plan and a letter, you agree. If offered options, you choose.

Findings, released when examined: comfortable; pulse 64 regular; blood pressure lying 128/80, standing 126/78; temperature 36.6 °C. Visual acuity normal in both eyes. Visual fields to confrontation: bitemporal loss. Fundi normal. Eye movements normal. Reduced facial hair; testes small and soft; no breast tissue or galactorrhoea; no acromegalic features.

Results, only when requested: prolactin about 25,400 mU/litre (1,200 micrograms/litre); testosterone low with low LH and FSH; 9 am cortisol 210 nmol/litre (indeterminate; short Synacthen test, if requested: 30-minute cortisol 340 nmol/litre, below 500); TSH low-normal with low free T4; IGF-1 normal. MRI: a pituitary macroadenoma touching the optic chiasm.

Question ladder: 1. Diagnosis? (D) 2. What do you make of the hormone results? (D) 3. What is first-line treatment? (E) Cabergoline. 4. Which hormone do you replace first, and how do you confirm the need? (E) Assess the adrenal axis before starting thyroxine; if this cannot be done promptly, give hydrocortisone cover first. A 9 am cortisol between about 83 and 415 nmol/litre is indeterminate, so confirm with a short Synacthen test (peak below 500 nmol/litre indicates adrenal insufficiency); if thyroxine cannot wait, cover with hydrocortisone until evaluated, and treat at once if he is unwell (Endocrine Society 2016, 1.3, 1.4, 2.20). 5. What are the driving rules? (E)

Curveballs: He says he will carry on driving: no; he must stop and tell DVLA, the Group 2 field standard is not met and a bitemporal defect is usually unacceptable for a car, and if he refuses the doctor may tell DVLA (GMC). Sudden severe headache with vomiting and falling vision: pituitary apoplexy, call 999. He asks about children: fertility may return with treatment.
Introduces self, asks consent and asks about discomfort before examining (G)
Asks about vision, sexual function and what he drives (C)
Tests the visual fields and checks the fundi (A)
Finds bitemporal field loss and signs of low testosterone (B)
Names a pituitary macroadenoma, probably a prolactinoma, with hypopituitarism (D)
Requests prolactin, testosterone, cortisol, thyroid function, MRI and formal fields (E)
Assesses the adrenal axis before starting thyroxine, with hydrocortisone cover first if that cannot be done promptly (E)
Says cabergoline is first-line and baseline echo is needed (E)
Says he must stop driving his lorry and car, tell DVLA, and gives red flags (E)
Asks what worries him and addresses his job and his fear of surgery (F)
Fail performance
CANDIDATE: Take your shirt off. [R1 Fail] Headaches, then? [R2 Fail]
CANDIDATE: (Skips the fields.) [R3 Fail] It's migraine. [R4 Fail] A scan only. [R5 Fail]
CANDIDATE: Carry on driving, and we'll book surgery. [R6 Fail] Don't worry. [R7 Fail] I'll tell you what we'll do. [R8 Fail]

Examiner note: Critical fail (AMaC practice flag, not an official automatic PACES fail): a lorry driver with bitemporal field loss must not drive. No consent, the fields skipped, migraine assumed, and his fears dismissed.
Pass performance
CANDIDATE: I'm the registrar. May I test your sight and check your blood pressure? Tell me if anything hurts. I'll cover you afterwards. [R1 Pass]
CANDIDATE: Where is the headache? Any loss of sight at the sides? Tired? Erections, libido, breast changes? Any tablets? What do you drive? [R2 Pass]
PATIENT: Forehead, for six months. I miss things at the sides. A lorry.
CANDIDATE: (Examines.) Loss of vision on both outer sides, normal fundi and eye movements, less facial hair, small soft testes. [R3 Pass]
CANDIDATE: A pituitary growth pressing on the sight nerves, probably a prolactinoma. [R4 Pass]
CANDIDATE: Prolactin, testosterone with LH and FSH, 9 am cortisol, thyroid tests, IGF-1, an MRI and formal fields. [R5 Pass]

CANDIDATE: Don't drive your lorry or your car until DVLA advise, and you must tell them. If the 9 am cortisol is indeterminate I'd confirm with a Synacthen test. I'd check the adrenal axis before any thyroid tablet, and if that can't be done quickly I'd cover with hydrocortisone first. Once confirmed, cabergoline, a tablet, is the usual treatment. Sudden severe headache means 999. [R6 Pass]
CANDIDATE: What worries you? [R7 Pass]
PATIENT: An operation, and losing my job.
CANDIDATE: Fair. A tablet is usually tried first, and I'll write to your firm. [R7 Pass] We can start tests and the tablet, or tests and an early surgical opinion. Which do you prefer? [R8 Pass]
Examiner note: Found the field loss, gave driving advice and a safety net. Did not name the baseline echo before cabergoline or the other causes of a raised prolactin.
High-performance performance
CANDIDATE: I'm the registrar. May I examine you? Would you like a chaperone? May I ask some personal questions about sex and fertility? [R1 High]
CANDIDATE: Any partner, thirst, or near misses on the road? [R2 High]
CANDIDATE: (Examines.) Normal acuity, no galactorrhoea, no acromegalic features, no postural fall. [R3 High]
CANDIDATE: A macroadenoma, probably a prolactinoma. A non-functioning tumour can raise prolactin by pressing on the stalk, and drugs can too. [R4 High]
CANDIDATE: The hormone tests, MRI, formal fields and a baseline echo before cabergoline. [R5 High]

CANDIDATE: Stop driving the lorry and your car until DVLA advise, and you must tell them; if you don't, GMC guidance means I may have to. I'd check the adrenal axis before any thyroid tablet, and if that can't be done quickly I'd cover with hydrocortisone first; surgery only if tablets fail or sight is threatened; 999 for sudden severe headache. [R6 High]
CANDIDATE: I'll write a letter for your employer and occupational health. [R7 High]
CANDIDATE: I'll give you a written summary and repeat your fields at the next visit. [R8 High]
Examiner note: Added a chaperone, fertility and near misses, the alternative cause, baseline echo, steroid-first replacement, the DVLA duty, an employer letter and a written plan.
R3: Not testing the visual fields. The bitemporal loss is the finding that decides his licence and the urgency.
R4: Calling it migraine. Headache with sexual loss and field loss points to a pituitary lesion.
R6: Letting him keep driving. A bitemporal field loss does not meet the lorry licence standard and is usually unacceptable for a car licence, and he has already nearly crashed.
R6: Starting thyroxine before the adrenal axis is assessed, or without hydrocortisone cover when assessment cannot be done promptly. In low cortisol it can provoke an adrenal crisis.
"Can I test your sight at the edges before I go on?"
"I should ask what you drive, because it affects my advice."
"I'd like to check I've understood what worries you most."

Endocrine Society 2011: a dopamine agonist is first-line for prolactinoma; cabergoline is preferred to bromocriptine for efficacy and tolerance. Stop a dopamine agonist when pregnancy is found. Exclude drug causes before MRI. Endocrine Society 2016: a 9 am cortisol below 3 micrograms/dL (83 nmol/litre) indicates adrenal insufficiency and above 15 (about 415) likely excludes it; between, do a corticotropin stimulation test (peak below 500 nmol/litre indicates insufficiency). Assess for adrenal insufficiency before starting levothyroxine in central hypothyroidism, with empirical glucocorticoid cover until evaluated.

Cabergoline is reasonable first-line even with field defects, unless acuity is threatened by rapid progression or haemorrhage, when surgery is needed. Baseline echocardiography before long-term treatment, repeated within 3 to 6 months and then every 6 to 12 months (MHRA Drug Safety Update, October 2008; cabergoline SmPC).

DVLA (last updated 26 September 2025): a visual field defect must be notified in Group 1 and Group 2. Group 1 needs a horizontal field of at least 120 degrees with no significant defect within 20 degrees of fixation, and bitemporal defects near fixation are usually unacceptable; Group 2 needs at least 160 degrees with no defect within 30 degrees of the centre. The duty to notify is the driver's; GMC guidance allows the doctor to disclose to DVLA if a patient who is unfit refuses to stop driving.
THINK: Headache, low libido, bitemporal loss: pituitary.
SAY: "A pituitary growth pressing on the sight nerves."
DO: Test fields; ask what he drives.
NUMBERS: Group 2 field of at least 160 degrees (DVLA).
TRAP: Forgetting the licence; sending to surgery.
FINISH: Cabergoline; assess the adrenal axis before any thyroxine (hydrocortisone cover first if not prompt); DVLA; 999 for sudden headache.

Melmed S et al. Diagnosis and treatment of hyperprolactinemia: an Endocrine Society clinical practice guideline. J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2011;96:273-288. https://doi.org/10.1210/jc.2010-1692 Supports: Dopamine agonist first-line, cabergoline preferred, stopping in pregnancy, drug causes.

Fleseriu M et al. Hormonal replacement in hypopituitarism in adults: an Endocrine Society clinical practice guideline. J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2016;101:3888-3921. https://doi.org/10.1210/jc.2016-2118 Supports: Morning cortisol thresholds, corticotropin stimulation test, and adrenal evaluation or glucocorticoid cover before levothyroxine.

Prolactinoma management. Endotext. https://www.endotext.org/wp-content/uploads/pdfs/prolactinoma-management.pdf Supports: Cabergoline with visual field defects, visual field monitoring and pituitary function tests. MHRA Drug Safety Update, Ergot-derived dopamine agonists: risk of fibrotic reactions (October 2008, republished December 2014), https://www.gov.uk/drug-safety-update/ergot-derived-dopamine-agonists-risk-of-fibrotic-reactions Supports: echocardiography before treatment, within 3 to 6 months, then every 6 to 12 months.

DVLA. Visual disorders: assessing fitness to drive (last updated 26 September 2025). https://www.gov.uk/guidance/visual-disorders-assessing-fitness-to-drive Supports: Notifying DVLA of a visual field defect; Group 2 field standards.

General Medical Council. Confidentiality: patients' fitness to drive and reporting concerns to the DVLA or DVA (2017). https://www.gmc-uk.org/professional-standards/the-professional-standards/confidentiality---patients-fitness-to-drive-and-reporting-concerns-to-the-dvla-or-dva Supports: the patient's duty to notify and when the doctor may disclose.
